```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
```

# Introduction
The Palmer Penguins dataset contains measurements of body mass (g), bill length (mm), bill depth (mm), and 
flipper length (mm) of three different species. The three species include, Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins
from Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Data was collected between the
years 2007 and 2009 by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program.
For this report, body mass and bill length differences between the sexes among the three species will be explored. 
(https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/articles/intro.html)

1. The dataset contains 344 penguin records with 8 columns: species, island, sex, year, bill length, bill depth, 
flipper length, and body mass.

2. Provide the name of a column for each data type in the data set   
Examples of each data type in the dataset are:
- Factor: `species`
- Numeric: `bill_length_mm`
- Integer: `flipper_length_mm`

3. How many penguins do we have data for?
344 penguins 

```{r sex-comparison}
# Count females, males, and records with missing sex.
table(penguins$sex, useNA = "ifany")

# Create a dataframe containing only male penguins.
pmale <- subset(penguins, sex == "male")

# Create a dataframe containing only female penguins.
pfemale <- subset(penguins, sex == "female")

# Check how many penguins are in each dataframe.
nrow(pmale)
nrow(pfemale)
```

4. Do we have equal representations of males and females in the dataset?
No, males and females are not in equal representation in the dataset. The dataset contains 168 male penguins and 
165 female penguins. However, there are 11 penguins with unspecified sex assignment, and thus, was excluded
from both subsets.

```{r species-comparison}
# Count the penguins belonging to each species.
table(penguins$species)

# Create a separate dataframe for each species.
pAdel <- subset(penguins, species == "Adelie")
pChin <- subset(penguins, species == "Chinstrap")
pGen <- subset(penguins, species == "Gentoo")

# Check the number of penguins in each new dataframe.
nrow(pAdel)
nrow(pChin)
nrow(pGen)
```

5. Do we have equal representation of each species in the dataset?
No, each species is not in equal representation in the dataset. The dataset contains 152 Adelie penguins, 
68 Chinstrap penguins, and 124 Gentoo penguins.

```{r island-comparison}
# Count the penguins recorded on each island.
table(penguins$island)

# Create a separate dataframe for each island.
iBis <- subset(penguins, island == "Biscoe")
iDream <- subset(penguins, island == "Dream")
iTorg <- subset(penguins, island == "Torgersen")

# Check the number of penguins in each new dataframe.
nrow(iBis)
nrow(iDream)
nrow(iTorg)
```

6. Do we have equal representation of each island in the dataset? 
No, each island is not in equal representation in the dataset. The dataset contains 168 penguins on Biscoe Island, 
124 penguins on Dream Island, and 52 penguins on Torgersen Island.

# Data visualization

## Exploring differences between males and females

```{r sex-exploration, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
# Keep records with sex information and arrange the four measurements
# so each measurement can appear in a separate panel.
sex_measurements <- pivot_longer(
  subset(penguins, !is.na(sex)),
  cols = c(
    bill_length_mm,
    bill_depth_mm,
    flipper_length_mm,
    body_mass_g
  ),
  names_to = "measurement",
  values_to = "value",
  values_drop_na = TRUE
)

# Compare females and males for each body measurement.
ggplot(
  sex_measurements,
  aes(x = sex, y = value, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ measurement,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 2,
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      bill_length_mm = "Bill length (mm)",
      bill_depth_mm = "Bill depth (mm)",
      flipper_length_mm = "Flipper length (mm)",
      body_mass_g = "Body mass (g)"
    ))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(female = "#B6B6B0", male = "#1F6F5F")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body measurements by recorded sex",
    x = "Recorded sex",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "All three species combined; missing sex or measurement excluded."
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


## Final comparison of body mass between sexes

```{r FINALsex, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Use records with both sex and body mass recorded.
sex_data <- subset(
  penguins,
  !is.na(sex) & !is.na(body_mass_g)
)

# Compare mean body mass using Welch's two-sample t-test.
sex_test <- t.test(
  body_mass_g ~ sex,
  data = sex_data,
  var.equal = FALSE
)

# Plot the same records used in the statistical test.
ggplot(
  sex_data,
  aes(x = sex, y = body_mass_g, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 3,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(female = "#B6B6B0", male = "#1F6F5F")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body mass by recorded sex",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Welch t-test p-value:",
      format.pval(sex_test$p.value, digits = 3)
    ),
    x = "Recorded sex",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    caption = paste(
      "White diamonds show means; box center lines show medians.",
      "All three species combined.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Display the test results for the written interpretation.
sex_test
```

Male penguins have a higher mean body mass of 4545.7 g, versus females that have a lower mean body mass of 3862.3 g. 
Welch's two-sample t-test demonstrated differences in mean body mass between male and female penguins 
(t = -8.55; df = 323.9; p < 0.001). Males were on average, 683.4 g heavier than females, with a 95% confidence interval for 
the male-female difference ranging from 526.2 g to 840.6 g. Although mean body mass differed between males and females, 
there was overlap in the distributions, indicating that individual variation is also important and body mass alone cannot 
entirely distinguish between the male and female penguins. The comparisons made here, however, did not adjust for the 
differences among the three species. 

## Exploring body measurements among species

```{r species-exploration, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
# Arrange the four body measurements into a separate table
# so each measurement can appear in its own panel.
species_measurements <- pivot_longer(
  penguins,
  cols = c(
    bill_length_mm,
    bill_depth_mm,
    flipper_length_mm,
    body_mass_g
  ),
  names_to = "measurement",
  values_to = "value",
  values_drop_na = TRUE
)

# Compare the distributions of each measurement among species.
ggplot(
  species_measurements,
  aes(x = species, y = value)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.6,
    fill = "#DDE9E5",
    colour = "#171717"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ measurement,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 2,
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      bill_length_mm = "Bill length (mm)",
      bill_depth_mm = "Bill depth (mm)",
      flipper_length_mm = "Flipper length (mm)",
      body_mass_g = "Body mass (g)"
    ))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body measurements by penguin species",
    x = "Species",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Missing measurements were omitted from the relevant panel."
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

# Scatterplot
## Final comparison of bill measurements among species

```{r FINALspecies, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
# Keep records with species and both bill measurements available.
species_data <- subset(
  penguins,
  !is.na(species) &
    !is.na(bill_length_mm) &
    !is.na(bill_depth_mm)
)

# Test species differences in the two bill measurements together.
species_model <- manova(
  cbind(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) ~ species,
  data = species_data
)

# Obtain Pillai's test statistic and its p-value.
species_test <- summary(species_model, test = "Pillai")
species_p <- species_test$stats["species", "Pr(>F)"]

# Calculate the mean bill measurements for each species.
species_means <- aggregate(
  cbind(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) ~ species,
  data = species_data,
  FUN = mean
)

# Plot individual penguins using colour and shape for species.
ggplot(
  species_data,
  aes(
    x = bill_length_mm,
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    colour = species,
    shape = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = species_means,
    aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 23,
    size = 4,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "#171717"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      Adelie = "#6F6F6F",
      Chinstrap = "#171717",
      Gentoo = "#1F6F5F"
    )
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(Adelie = 16, Chinstrap = 17, Gentoo = 15)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Bill measurements by penguin species",
    subtitle = paste(
      "MANOVA using Pillai's trace; p-value:",
      format.pval(species_p, digits = 3)
    ),
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Bill depth (mm)",
    colour = "Species",
    shape = "Species",
    caption = paste(
      "Points represent individual penguins; white diamonds show species means.",
      "Records with missing bill measurements were excluded.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

# Display the statistical results for the written interpretation.
species_test
```

# Interpretation/conclusion of the statistical test

Bill length and depth are of considerable difference when compared across penguin species. MANOVA using Pillai's 
trace showed strong differences in the combined mean bill measurements (Pillai's trace = 1.2714, approximate 
F(4, 678) = 295.78, p < 0.001). In the scatterplot, the Adelie penguins generally had 
shorter bills than both the Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins. Chinstrap penguins demonstrated
relatively long, deep bills, while the Gentoo penguins had the longest and most shallow bills overall.
These observations helped to distinguish between the species, although some individual measurements
overlapped. The overall MANOVA result indicates that at least one of the species differed
in its mean combination of bill characteristics and associated measurements. However, it does not
establish that each species pair differed significantly or that these measurements identify every individual
correctly. Therefore, while the MANOVA provides evidence of overall differences between species, 
it should be interpreted with caution and supplemented with additional analyses if needed. This analysis
did not adjust for potential confounding variables or multiple comparisons, which could affect the interpretation 
of the results, for instance, sex, island (i.e., variable conditions across different islands), or year (i.e., 
different conditions depending on the year of observation).
